doc.title: Lanny Morgan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Lean New York years after the band broke up
summary: After 1966 he did a demo, jingles, a Long Island club, teaching and Howard McGhee's band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. Good to be a part of it. You came back, was it a conscious decision to come back and get into studio work on your part or did you just kind of fall into it?

Well I didn’t really, I didn’t have a thought of ever coming back to Los Angeles. But you know things had fallen to almost zero in New York. Maynard left in 1966 and I had a little group with Mike Abene and Ronnie McClure, Antonio Zalocco and a trumpet player named Dick Hurwitz, had a little quintet, and we made a demo, we had made a demo earlier, before the band broke up that I couldn’t sell, and I still have it, it’s a good demo, it really is. But I took it to Neshui Ertegun once on a cold winter’s night and he gave me this jive about how the company didn’t have any money and he had his feet on the desk and was talking on the phone while he was listening to my platter, you know it was like a pancake style. And he said he didn’t have any money and the next couple of weeks they released some of the worst horseshit that I ever heard in my life. But that was my introduction to the record business. You know you don’t just bring them something good and say, “I’d like to have you do this,” because there’s more to it than that. But anyway that fell through and that was kind of discouraging. And then I was doing some jingles in New York. Mike Abene had gotten a little bit into the jingle end of it writing for them and he got me in on some of those, just a little bit of this and that, some record dates. I was working at a supper club in Mineola, Long Island that took up the slack. I mean I had a deal there where if I wasn’t working I could always go in there and do it, and that was good for three or four nights a week. I had probably 30 private students and I drove to their house and that really broke my back, that was really difficult.
Wow. This was in New York?

In New York, on Long Island. And I charged, I worked for a company and they charged them $5.00 and out of that I got $3.50. So I mean what is that, thirty students, if I taught them all in a week, that was 90, a little less than a hundred dollars. And then I started to work a gig, the Copacabana opened up and I took that for about the last nine months I was in New York. But you know even the jazz thing kind of folded it seemed like. I was on a band that Howard McGhee put together for a couple of years. And we used to play festivals and things. We rehearsed at that church that the Reverend Gensel had on Fifth Avenue was it or Madison?
